title: Finite-precision transformer resource bounds
open: Establish tight depth, width, numerical-precision, and context-length trade-offs for transformers solving explicitly specified algorithmic task families. Include external scratchpads and recurrent execution rather than assuming either unlimited precision or a single fixed-depth pass.
status: The modern theory includes restricted-model limitations dating to 2019 and constructive scratchpad results from 2021. These do not provide a unified, practically predictive resource hierarchy.
why: Separates architectural impossibility from insufficient training or inadequate computation.
key_works: Hahn, 2019/2020, *Theoretical Limitations of Self-Attention in Neural Sequence Models*, arXiv:1906.06755; Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models*, arXiv:2112.00114.

title: Identifying the mechanism of natural-language in-context learning
open: Determine when an LLM’s in-context behavior is best explained by Bayesian inference, optimization, retrieval, pattern completion, or combinations of these. A solution should make interventionally testable predictions on natural-language tasks, not only fit behavior on synthetic regression.
status: Bayesian accounts and controlled function-learning demonstrations appeared in 2021–2022. Their applicability and relative contribution in heterogeneous pretrained models remain incompletely characterized.
why: Enables predictable prompting and principled selection of demonstrations.
key_works: Xie et al., 2021/2022, *An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference*, arXiv:2111.02080; Garg et al., 2022, *What Can Transformers Learn In-Context?*, arXiv:2208.01066.

title: Learning algorithms that extrapolate beyond training lengths
open: Identify training distributions and inductive biases that produce algorithms whose correctness persists at substantially greater input lengths. Require performance curves and, where possible, guarantees beyond the lengths used for training and model selection.
status: Systematic-generalization failures have been studied since at least 2017; scratchpads provide a useful partial mechanism. Success on selected arithmetic tasks does not establish general length extrapolation.
why: Supports reliable reasoning over larger programs, documents, graphs, and proofs.
key_works: Lake and Baroni, 2017/2018, *Generalization without systematicity*, arXiv:1711.00350; Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114.

title: Predicting grokking before generalization occurs
open: Predict whether, when, and on which distributions a memorizing network will transition to generalization, using measurements available before that transition. The predictor should transfer across tasks, optimizers, architectures, and training scales.
status: Grokking was documented in 2022 on small algorithmic datasets. Explaining individual examples is weaker than forecasting transition times and distinguishing eventual generalization from permanent overfitting.
why: Could avoid wasted training and reveal which internal structures support abstraction.
key_works: Power et al., 2022, *Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets*, arXiv:2201.02177.

title: Deployment-relevant generalization certificates
open: Produce computable generalization bounds that meaningfully predict downstream error, including important distribution shifts, for practically trained LLMs. Bounds should distinguish better from worse models rather than merely fall below a trivial ceiling.
status: Non-vacuous bounds already exist: 2023 work addressed large compressed models, and 2024 token-level bounds reached compressed LLaMA2-70B. The remaining target is tightness and deployment relevance, not the existence of any non-vacuous bound.
why: Provides a mathematical complement to benchmark-based assurance.
key_works: Lotfi et al., 2023, *Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds for Large Language Models*, arXiv:2312.17173; Lotfi et al., 2024, *Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models*, arXiv:2407.18158.

title: Distinguishing genuine capability transitions from measurement artifacts
open: Develop tests that distinguish a real qualitative change in learned computation from thresholding, discontinuous scoring, contamination, or sparse sampling of model sizes. Specify what observations would falsify an emergence claim.
status: The 2023 “mirage” analysis demonstrated that some apparent emergence depends on metric choice. It does not establish that every qualitative transition is an artifact.
why: Improves scaling forecasts and prevents misleading capability narratives.
key_works: Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo, 2023, *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, arXiv:2304.15004; Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361.

title: Implicit bias in feature-learning language models
open: Characterize which functions realistic optimizers select in the feature-learning regime of large language models, including the effects of normalization, adaptive updates, finite precision, and data ordering. Derive consequences for robustness and generalization.
status: Precise implicit-bias results exist for restricted settings, including separable linear classification. Those results do not yet determine the effective bias of full-scale transformer training.
why: Makes optimization choices interpretable as choices about the solution learned.
key_works: Soudry et al., 2017/2018, *The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data*, arXiv:1710.10345; Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Identifiable causal representations from language and interaction
open: State sufficient and necessary conditions under which language, demonstrations, and interventions identify useful causal variables rather than merely predictive latent factors. Algorithms should recover those variables up to a clearly specified equivalence class.
status: Causal representation learning has a substantial theoretical agenda, articulated in 2021. General identification from observational text alone is not supplied by that agenda.
why: Supports intervention planning, counterfactual reasoning, and robust transfer.
key_works: Schölkopf et al., 2021, *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Locatello et al., 2018/2019, *Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations*, arXiv:1811.12359.

title: Lifetime-compute-optimal model design
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Jointly choose parameter count, training tokens, architecture, compression, and serving strategy to minimize lifetime cost for a specified demand distribution and quality requirement. Include retraining and model retirement rather than optimizing pretraining alone.
status: Chinchilla established a prominent training-compute baseline in 2022. Inference-aware scaling studies in 2025 explicitly extend the objective, but workload-dependent lifetime optimization remains broader.
why: Prevents choosing models that are cheap to train but expensive to operate.
key_works: Hoffmann et al., 2022, *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; Bian et al., 2025, *Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models*, arXiv:2501.18107.

title: Scaling-law transfer across domains
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Predict downstream capability from small experiments when the target domain, data mixture, or evaluation distribution differs substantially from the fitted scaling regime. Predictions should include calibrated extrapolation uncertainty.
status: Power-law descriptions date to 2020; subsequent work tests overtraining and downstream-task scaling. Reliable transfer to new domains and architectures is a stronger requirement than interpolation within a training family.
why: Reduces expensive failed training programs.
key_works: Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361; Gadre et al., 2024, *Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks*, arXiv:2403.08540.

title: Quality-adjusted data scaling laws
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Replace raw token counts with a measurable account of novelty, correctness, diversity, and task relevance that predicts marginal training value. The measure must remain useful when the model and data mixture change.
status: DoReMi and DataComp-LM provide controlled mixture and filtering experiments from 2023–2024. Neither raw corpus size nor a universal scalar “quality score” fully resolves the target.
why: Directs acquisition and curation toward information rather than volume.
key_works: Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining*, arXiv:2305.10429; Li et al., 2024, *DataComp-LM*, arXiv:2406.11794.

title: Hyperparameter transfer across architectural changes
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Transfer learning rates, initialization, regularization, and optimizer settings across simultaneous changes in width, depth, sequence length, precision, and architecture. Quantify where transfer fails and supply inexpensive corrective measurements.
status: μP demonstrated valuable zero-shot transfer across model widths in 2022. A general transfer rule covering all of these changes is a substantially stronger target.
why: Cuts the cost and instability of scaling experiments.
key_works: Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Early warning of catastrophic training instability
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Detect impending loss spikes, numerical overflow, expert collapse, or irreversible representation damage early enough to intervene. A solution should predict failures across training runs without an excessive false-alarm rate.
status: Large-model reports document practical stabilization techniques, including low-precision and mixture-of-experts training. A transferable failure-prediction benchmark and intervention policy remain separate targets.
why: Avoids losing expensive training progress and silently degraded checkpoints.
key_works: DeepSeek-AI, 2024, *DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report*, arXiv:2412.19437; Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Joint quality–latency scaling laws for sparse experts
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Predict quality, communication cost, utilization, and tail latency jointly as expert count, active parameters, routing policy, and hardware topology change. Include rare-token and distribution-shift behavior.
status: Routed-model scaling laws appeared in 2022; later sparse architectures improve specialization. These are partial answers, not a universal hardware-aware law.
why: Makes sparse architectures easier to select and deploy economically.
key_works: Clark et al., 2022, *Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models*, arXiv:2202.01169; Dai et al., 2024, *DeepSeekMoE*, arXiv:2401.06066.

title: Optimal allocation between pretraining, post-training, and inference
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Allocate a fixed total budget among pretraining, supervised tuning, reinforcement learning, verifier training, and test-time search. Optimize a specified portfolio of tasks rather than one benchmark.
status: Test-time scaling studies and reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning demonstrate different productive spending directions. Their joint marginal returns are not captured by one generally reliable allocation rule.
why: Determines where the next unit of compute creates the most value.
key_works: Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314; DeepSeek-AI, 2025, *DeepSeek-R1*, arXiv:2501.12948.

title: Tenfold reduction in unique training-data requirements
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Match a preregistered baseline’s broad, contamination-controlled performance using at most one-tenth as much unique training data, without hiding equivalent information in teachers or synthetic-data generators.
status: Data-mixture optimization and large-scale curation provide measurable improvements. A broad tenfold information-efficiency improvement under explicit information accounting is the proposed moonshot.
why: Makes capable models feasible for domains and languages with scarce data.
key_works: Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi*, arXiv:2305.10429; Penedo et al., 2024, *The FineWeb Datasets*, arXiv:2406.17557.

title: Causal valuation of individual training examples
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Estimate how adding, removing, or modifying a training example changes downstream behavior, with uncertainty and validation against retraining. Scale this to nonlinear training pipelines containing duplicates and interacting examples.
status: Influence-function methods established useful approximations in 2017. Faithful attribution through large-scale, nonconvex, multistage training remains a stronger task.
why: Supports debugging, compensation, privacy remediation, and targeted data collection.
key_works: Koh and Liang, 2017, *Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions*, arXiv:1703.04730.

title: Adaptive data mixtures without benchmark overfitting
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Continuously adapt data sampling to a model’s learning needs while preserving minority capabilities and avoiding overfitting the mixture controller to evaluation tasks.
status: DoReMi demonstrated distributionally robust mixture optimization in 2023. Extending adaptive mixtures across long training runs, changing objectives, and protected capability floors remains open.
why: Improves training efficiency without sacrificing less common domains.
key_works: Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining*, arXiv:2305.10429.

title: Semantic decontamination of training corpora
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Detect benchmark leakage through paraphrases, translations, worked solutions, generated derivatives, and structurally equivalent tasks. Quantify both missed leakage and excessive removal of legitimate training material.
status: Contamination-limited evaluations and standardized data pipelines address parts of the problem. Exact-string and near-duplicate checks do not certify semantic independence.
why: Makes measured generalization more credible.
key_works: White et al., 2024, *LiveBench*, arXiv:2406.19314; Li et al., 2024, *DataComp-LM*, arXiv:2406.11794.

title: Stability conditions for recursive synthetic-data training
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Characterize when repeated training on model-generated data preserves, improves, or destroys useful distributional information. Include finite data, selective filtering, changing model capacity, and imperfect access to real observations.
status: Collapse was demonstrated in 2023 settings; 2024 work showed that accumulating real and synthetic data can avoid it. Universal inevitability is therefore not the open claim.
why: Determines whether synthetic-data ecosystems remain sustainable.
key_works: Shumailov et al., 2023, *The Curse of Recursion*, arXiv:2305.17493; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024, *Is Model Collapse Inevitable?*, arXiv:2404.01413.

title: Preserving rare tails during synthetic augmentation
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Preserve rare but important facts, dialects, failure cases, and decision boundaries across repeated synthetic augmentation. Demonstrate tail preservation separately from average benchmark performance.
status: Recursive-training studies identify distributional degradation, while accumulation mitigates some collapse regimes. Tail-specific guarantees and realistic rare-event evaluations remain distinct targets.
why: Prevents apparently improving models from becoming less useful to uncommon users and cases.
key_works: Shumailov et al., 2023, *The Curse of Recursion*, arXiv:2305.17493; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024, *Is Model Collapse Inevitable?*, arXiv:2404.01413.

title: Machine-verifiable training-data rights lineage
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Preserve verifiable provenance, consent, attribution, and usage restrictions through scraping, transformation, deduplication, mixing, and synthetic derivation. Support correction and revocation without assuming every source has clean metadata.
status: The Data Provenance Initiative audited licensing and attribution in 2023 and expanded across modalities in 2024. Auditing existing gaps is not equivalent to maintaining end-to-end lineage.
why: Enables accountable dataset construction and more defensible reuse.
key_works: Longpre et al., 2023, *The Data Provenance Initiative*, arXiv:2310.16787; Longpre et al., 2024, *Bridging the Data Provenance Gap Across Text, Speech and Video*, arXiv:2412.17847.

title: Quality filtering without cultural erasure
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Design filters that remove genuinely low-value or harmful training material without disproportionately discarding dialects, minority viewpoints, informal writing, or low-resource languages. Evaluate downstream losses, not only retained-token statistics.
status: Large-scale filtering pipelines and linguistic-inclusion analyses provide starting points. A filter’s apparent quality gains can be assessed independently of its representational consequences.
why: Avoids building capability gaps into the corpus before training begins.
key_works: Penedo et al., 2024, *The FineWeb Datasets*, arXiv:2406.17557; Joshi et al., 2020, *The State and Fate of Linguistic Diversity and Inclusion in the NLP World*, arXiv:2004.09095.

title: Reusable private-domain research corpora
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Create privacy-preserving, legally reusable corpora for domains such as enterprise workflows and professional correspondence, with realistic longitudinal tasks and independent evaluation access. Preserve utility that aggressive anonymization can destroy.
status: Dataset documentation and provenance frameworks exist. They do not themselves supply access arrangements, privacy guarantees, or representative private-workflow data.
why: Reduces dependence on unrealistic public-web substitutes for real work.
key_works: Gebru et al., 2018/2021, *Datasheets for Datasets*, arXiv:1803.09010; Longpre et al., 2024, *Bridging the Data Provenance Gap*, arXiv:2412.17847.

title: Recurrent-state memory–accuracy frontiers
open: Determine the achievable trade-off between recurrent-state size, update cost, and recovery of task-relevant historical information. Separate arbitrary exact recall—which has elementary storage limits—from realistic distribution-dependent recall.
status: Mamba demonstrated selective state-space modeling in 2023. Its efficiency does not settle optimal memory allocation or retrieval fidelity across arbitrary long-running tasks.
why: Supports long-lived agents without ever-growing attention caches.
key_works: Gu and Dao, 2023, *Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces*, arXiv:2312.00752.

title: Input-adaptive recurrent computation
open: Learn how much internal computation each input or reasoning state needs, with reliable stopping and no pathological infinite loops. Compare against fixed-depth models under matched latency and energy budgets.
status: Scratchpads and latent reasoning show routes to additional computation. A broadly reliable controller for allocating and terminating that computation remains a separate target.
why: Spends expensive reasoning only where it improves outcomes.
key_works: Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114; Hao et al., 2024, *Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space*, arXiv:2412.06769.

title: Positional representations with controlled extrapolation failure
open: Characterize positional encodings that preserve specified computations beyond training lengths, and prove necessary resource growth where extrapolation is impossible. Include finite precision and changing sampling density.
status: Rotary position embeddings provide a widely studied 2021 construction. A positional mechanism alone does not guarantee algorithmic extrapolation or immunity to numerical aliasing.
why: Distinguishes fixable context-extension failures from structural limits.
key_works: Su et al., 2021, *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding*, arXiv:2104.09864; Hahn, 2019/2020, *Theoretical Limitations of Self-Attention*, arXiv:1906.06755.

title: Adaptive byte-level modeling without language penalties
open: Learn variable-rate segmentation that preserves multilingual quality, handles corrupted or novel strings, and allocates computation according to information content rather than tokenizer accidents.
status: Byte Latent Transformer explored dynamic byte patching at scales up to 8 billion parameters in 2024. Robustness, efficiency, and language equity must still be jointly demonstrated.
why: Reduces tokenizer brittleness and uneven costs across writing systems.
key_works: Pagnoni et al., 2024, *Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens*, arXiv:2412.09871; Petrov et al., 2023, *Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages*, arXiv:2305.15425.

title: Auditable continuous latent reasoning
open: Make continuous internal reasoning states inspectable, interruptible, and verifiable without forcing every useful computation into natural-language tokens. Detect when a latent computation violates a task constraint.
status: Coconut demonstrated a concrete continuous-latent reasoning approach, with revisions through 2026. Demonstrated task gains do not constitute general interpretability or safety assurance.
why: Retains computational efficiency without losing meaningful oversight.
key_works: Hao et al., 2024, *Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space*, arXiv:2412.06769; Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702.

title: Diffusion language models with competitive interactive serving
open: Achieve competitive quality, time to first useful output, incremental revision, and total serving cost with diffusion-based language generation. Evaluate streaming and tool-use workloads, not only offline text completion.
status: LLaDA demonstrated large-scale masked-diffusion language modeling in 2025. Interactive serving imposes a different optimization problem from batch generation.
why: Tests whether non-autoregressive generation can improve practical applications.
key_works: Nie et al., 2025, *Large Language Diffusion Models*, arXiv:2502.09992.

title: Stable and interpretable expert specialization
open: Induce expert specialization that remains useful under domain shift, resists routing collapse, and can be updated without damaging unrelated experts. Measure genuine functional specialization rather than routing labels alone.
status: DeepSeekMoE and routed-model scaling work provide architectural and empirical progress. Stable modularity across training stages and deployment shifts remains a stronger requirement.
why: Could make large models cheaper to update, debug, and customize.
key_works: Dai et al., 2024, *DeepSeekMoE*, arXiv:2401.06066; Clark et al., 2022, *Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models*, arXiv:2202.01169.

title: Architecture-level communication lower bounds
open: Derive tight memory-traffic and inter-device communication bounds for complete model execution, including attention, experts, normalization, and decoding state. Identify architectures that approach these bounds on realistic hardware.
status: FlashAttention established important I/O-aware improvements for exact attention in 2022–2023. Whole-model and distributed lower bounds remain broader than attention-kernel optimization.
why: Reveals which efficiency gains require architectural change rather than kernel tuning.
key_works: Dao et al., 2022, *FlashAttention*, arXiv:2205.14135; Dao, 2023, *FlashAttention-2*, arXiv:2307.08691.

title: Reward optimization without proxy collapse
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Optimize learned rewards while maintaining improvement on independently measured human objectives, even as optimization pressure exceeds the reward model’s training regime. Detect the onset of overoptimization before substantial damage.
status: Reward-model overoptimization was systematically studied in 2022. Better reward models and regularization are partial defenses, not a universal guarantee.
why: Prevents stronger optimization from producing worse real behavior.
key_works: Gao, Schulman, and Hilton, 2022, *Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization*, arXiv:2210.10760; Lambert et al., 2024, *RewardBench*, arXiv:2403.13787.

title: Learning from inconsistent and plural preferences
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Learn useful policies when preferences are context-dependent, nontransitive, and heterogeneous across people. Preserve disagreement rather than manufacturing an unjustified single global ranking.
status: DPO supplies a tractable preference-learning objective; pluralistic-alignment work explicitly treats disagreement as substantive. General aggregation and optimization guarantees remain unsettled.
why: Avoids equating one aggregate preference score with universal acceptability.
key_works: Rafailov et al., 2023, *Direct Preference Optimization*, arXiv:2305.18290; Sorensen et al., 2024, *A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment*, arXiv:2402.05070.

title: Distinguishing RL-driven discovery from probability redistribution
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Determine when post-training learns genuinely new reusable algorithms rather than reallocating probability toward solutions already accessible to the base model. Define “new” operationally and control for sampling budget and verifier effects.
status: DeepSeek-R1 and 2025 analyses of reasoning-capacity changes provide competing empirical perspectives. Results on particular benchmarks do not settle the general mechanism.
why: Clarifies the limits and potential of reinforcement learning after pretraining.
key_works: DeepSeek-AI, 2025, *DeepSeek-R1*, arXiv:2501.12948; Yue et al., 2025, *Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?*, arXiv:2504.13837.

title: Credit assignment across long tool-using trajectories
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Attribute delayed success or failure to the relevant reasoning steps, information-gathering actions, and external calls. Train on long trajectories without rewarding merely plausible intermediate explanations.
status: Process supervision provides a demonstrated approach for mathematical reasoning; tool-agent benchmarks introduce longer interactive trajectories. Their combination leaves difficult causal credit-assignment questions.
why: Enables learning from complex work rather than isolated answers.
key_works: Lightman et al., 2023, *Let’s Verify Step by Step*, arXiv:2305.20050; Yao et al., 2024, *τ-bench*, arXiv:2406.12045.

title: Stable online preference adaptation
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Adapt to a user’s evolving preferences without amplifying transient moods, manipulation, or accidental feedback. Bound regressions and distinguish durable preferences from situational instructions.
status: Offline preference optimization is well developed relative to this longitudinal target. Pluralistic alignment clarifies the need for context and individual variation.
why: Makes personalization useful without turning it into uncontrolled behavioral drift.
key_works: Rafailov et al., 2023, *Direct Preference Optimization*, arXiv:2305.18290; Sorensen et al., 2024, *A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment*, arXiv:2402.05070.

title: Post-training without hidden capability interference
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Predict and prevent unwanted interactions between task tuning, safety tuning, style tuning, and multilingual performance. Require capability-specific regression tests rather than relying on an aggregate score.
status: Model averaging and preference tuning show that behavioral modification is practical. They do not establish compositional preservation of independently desired capabilities.
why: Reduces the recurring cost of fixing one behavior while breaking another.
key_works: Wortsman et al., 2022, *Model soups*, arXiv:2203.05482; Rafailov et al., 2023, *Direct Preference Optimization*, arXiv:2305.18290.

title: Process supervision that rewards genuine progress
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Train process evaluators that identify causally useful reasoning steps and remain robust when generators optimize against them. Distinguish correct-looking narration from computation that actually supports the answer.
status: Step-level supervision improved mathematical reasoning in 2023 work. Faithfulness studies show why textual plausibility alone cannot establish a faithful process.
why: Makes intermediate supervision a reliable signal rather than another proxy to exploit.
key_works: Lightman et al., 2023, *Let’s Verify Step by Step*, arXiv:2305.20050; Turpin et al., 2023, *Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think*, arXiv:2305.04388.

title: Useful generalization guarantees for verifiable-reward RL
subfield: Post-training, preference learning, and reward design
open: Bound out-of-distribution performance after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, including adaptive task generation, verifier imperfections, and substantial parameter updates.
status: A July 2026 study provides non-vacuous bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR on billion-scale models. Extending useful guarantees beyond that setting is the residual target.
why: Connects successful post-training recipes to explicit limits on deployment risk.
key_works: Zhu, Alur, and Kang, 2026, *Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards*, arXiv:2607.14506.

title: Systematic compositional generalization
open: Generalize to withheld combinations of familiar primitives while controlling for lexical similarity, template leakage, and training distribution. Demonstrate transfer across multiple task families rather than one synthetic split.
status: SCAN made this failure mode explicit in 2017–2018. Task-specific progress does not settle general compositional learning.
why: Supports reliable reuse of known skills in unfamiliar combinations.
key_works: Lake and Baroni, 2017/2018, *Generalization without systematicity*, arXiv:1711.00350; Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610.

title: Consistent learning of invertible relations
open: When a relation is explicitly invertible, learn both directions and their compositions without separately enumerating each phrasing. Avoid incorrectly treating noninvertible relations as symmetric.
status: The 2023 reversal-curse experiments exposed failures to recover inverse associations from one-directional training. Robust solutions must generalize beyond the original experimental templates.
why: Improves relational knowledge access and reduces brittle fact memorization.
key_works: Berglund et al., 2023, *The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A”*, arXiv:2309.12288.

title: Reliable extrapolation of learned procedures
open: Learn procedures that remain correct as numerical magnitude, nesting depth, or graph size increases beyond training. Identify whether failures arise from representation, execution length, or learned shortcuts.
status: Scratchpads provide a useful execution format, but bounded benchmark success is not a general proof of procedural extrapolation.
why: Makes neural reasoning usable for workloads with unpredictable complexity.
key_works: Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114; Hahn, 2019/2020, *Theoretical Limitations of Self-Attention*, arXiv:1906.06755.

title: Robust reasoning under imperfect verifiers
open: Maintain sound outcomes when verifiers have implementation bugs, incomplete specifications, or correlated blind spots. Distinguish genuine proof from exploiting a checker or formalization error.
status: LeanDojo supplies a concrete theorem-proving infrastructure. A proof assistant can check a formal statement without guaranteeing that the statement captures the intended claim.
why: Prevents verification from becoming a false assurance layer.
key_works: Yang et al., 2023, *LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models*, arXiv:2306.15626; Gao et al., 2022, *Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization*, arXiv:2210.10760.

title: Selective self-correction with positive expected value
open: Decide when an initial answer should be retained, checked, revised, or escalated. Demonstrate net improvement after accounting for correct answers spoiled by unnecessary revision.
status: A 2023 study documented failures of unaided self-correction; this is historical evidence, not an impossibility theorem. The broader target is reliable selective correction across tasks.
why: Turns reflection from a ritual into an evidence-based control policy.
key_works: Huang et al., 2023/2024, *Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet*, arXiv:2310.01798; Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally*, arXiv:2408.03314.

title: Optimal stopping for test-time reasoning
open: Stop reasoning when expected improvement no longer justifies added latency, expense, or risk. Estimate this online without knowing the correct answer or using an oracle difficulty label.
status: Test-time compute allocation has demonstrated gains since 2024. A transferable stopping policy with reliable uncertainty remains a distinct target.
why: Avoids both premature answers and expensive unproductive deliberation.
key_works: Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314.

title: Planning with stochastic and exogenous changes
open: Construct and revise plans when actions have uncertain effects and the world changes independently of the agent. Evaluate belief updates and recovery, not only generation of a plausible static plan.
status: Planning evaluations from 2023 exposed weaknesses in classical planning tasks; interactive benchmarks extend the setting. Open-world stochastic planning is the stronger target.
why: Enables reliable execution outside deterministic demonstrations.
key_works: Valmeekam et al., 2023, *On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models*, arXiv:2305.15771; Yao et al., 2022/2023, *ReAct*, arXiv:2210.03629.

title: Counterfactual reasoning with explicit identification limits
open: Answer intervention and counterfactual questions only when justified by the available causal assumptions and evidence. Otherwise identify the missing assumptions or return an identified range.
status: LLM causal-reasoning studies appeared prominently in 2023. Linguistic plausibility does not by itself establish causal identification.
why: Prevents unsupported causal conclusions in science, medicine, and policy.
key_works: Kıcıman et al., 2023, *Causal Reasoning and Large Language Models*, arXiv:2305.00050; Schölkopf et al., 2021, *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107.

title: Evidence-complete retrieval
open: Retrieve enough evidence to support all material parts of an answer, including evidence that contradicts the apparent conclusion. Measure missing evidence separately from irrelevant retrieved material.
status: RAG established an influential retrieval–generation architecture in 2020. Accurate retrieval of some relevant passages is not a completeness certificate.
why: Reduces answers that are well cited but substantively incomplete.
key_works: Lewis et al., 2020, *Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks*, arXiv:2005.11401; Min et al., 2023, *FActScore*, arXiv:2305.14251.

title: Multi-hop retrieval without compounding search errors
open: Plan retrieval steps whose later queries depend on earlier findings while preserving alternative hypotheses and recovering from misleading early results.
status: Interleaved retrieval and reasoning were demonstrated in 2022–2023. The open target is robust search under incomplete, noisy, and branching evidence.
why: Supports complex investigations rather than single-fact lookup.
key_works: Trivedi et al., 2022/2023, *Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions*, arXiv:2212.10509.

title: Resolving contradictory sources without arbitrary authority heuristics
open: Reconcile conflicting evidence using provenance, methodology, temporal validity, and uncertainty. Preserve unresolved disagreement rather than silently choosing the most frequent or fluent source.
status: RAG and citation-generation systems expose evidence to generators, but source conflict requires additional epistemic and temporal reasoning.
why: Makes grounded answers useful in contested and rapidly changing domains.
key_works: Lewis et al., 2020, *Retrieval-Augmented Generation*, arXiv:2005.11401; Gao, Fisch, and Chen, 2023, *Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations*, arXiv:2305.14627.

title: Detecting that the corpus cannot answer the question
open: Distinguish “not retrieved,” “not present,” “not inferable,” and “contradicted” for a requested claim. Calibrate abstention while permitting justified inference from multiple documents.
status: Grounding and factuality benchmarks assess supporting evidence, but negative evidence and corpus insufficiency demand their own labels and evaluation.
why: Prevents fabricated answers when a private knowledge base lacks the answer.
key_works: Min et al., 2023, *FActScore*, arXiv:2305.14251; Gao et al., 2023, *Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations*, arXiv:2305.14627.

title: Claim-level citation entailment
open: Ensure each citation actually supports its attached claim, including qualifiers, quantities, and causal language. Detect citations that are relevant to the topic but do not entail the stated conclusion.
status: ALCE and FActScore introduced useful citation and atomic-factuality evaluation in 2023. Full compositional entailment remains more demanding than citation presence.
why: Makes citations evidence rather than decoration.
key_works: Gao et al., 2023, *Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations*, arXiv:2305.14627; Min et al., 2023, *FActScore*, arXiv:2305.14251.

title: Reliable joins across text, tables, and graphs
open: Answer questions requiring entity resolution and joins across narrative documents, relational tables, and knowledge graphs. Return auditable intermediate bindings and detect ambiguous joins.
status: GraphRAG demonstrated graph-assisted global summarization in 2024. Correct multi-representation joins are a different, more structured requirement.
why: Enables dependable enterprise and scientific knowledge integration.
key_works: Edge et al., 2024, *From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization*, arXiv:2404.16130.

title: Time-consistent knowledge grounding
open: Answer using the facts valid at the requested time, distinguishing publication time, event time, and later corrections. Support “what was knowable then?” as well as “what is true now?”
status: Retrieval and memory benchmarks address pieces of knowledge access and updates. Temporal consistency across sources and revisions remains an additional target.
why: Prevents anachronistic answers and supports audit reconstruction.
key_works: Lewis et al., 2020, *Retrieval-Augmented Generation*, arXiv:2005.11401; Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813.

title: Cross-lingual evidence retrieval without semantic loss
open: Retrieve and synthesize evidence across languages while preserving legal, technical, cultural, and numerical distinctions. Measure whether translation changes the conclusion or excludes relevant local sources.
status: Multilingual translation has advanced substantially; 2026 cross-lingual workflow evaluations expose a separate long-horizon agent challenge.
why: Makes knowledge access less dependent on the language of the query.
key_works: NLLB Team, 2022, *No Language Left Behind*, arXiv:2207.04672; Li et al., 2026, *PolyWorkBench*, arXiv:2607.06008.

title: Position-invariant use of relevant context
open: Preserve answer quality when relevant evidence moves within a long context, while holding content and distractors constant. Extend evaluation beyond single-needle retrieval to multi-evidence reasoning.
status: “Lost in the Middle” documented position sensitivity in 2023. Longer advertised context windows do not themselves establish position-invariant reasoning.
why: Makes document order less likely to determine correctness.
key_works: Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*, arXiv:2307.03172; Bai et al., 2023, *LongBench*, arXiv:2308.14508.

title: Task-sufficient context compression
open: Compress histories while preserving the information needed for a specified family of future questions and actions. Quantify distortion and identify when no compact sufficient representation exists.
status: Memory-managed agent architectures provide practical compression and paging mechanisms. They do not establish task-sufficiency guarantees for future unknown queries.
why: Reduces context cost without silently losing critical constraints.
key_works: Packer et al., 2023, *MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems*, arXiv:2310.08560; Gu and Dao, 2023, *Mamba*, arXiv:2312.00752.

title: Learning what to remember
open: Select which experiences should enter persistent memory based on future usefulness, privacy, uncertainty, and maintenance cost. Evaluate decisions before the future queries are revealed.
status: MemGPT and longitudinal memory benchmarks supply mechanisms and tests. Optimal prospective memory selection remains distinct from retrieving an already curated memory store.
why: Prevents memory systems from becoming expensive, noisy transcript archives.
key_works: Packer et al., 2023, *MemGPT*, arXiv:2310.08560; Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753.

title: Revising memories without losing historical truth
open: Update beliefs when facts change or earlier information is corrected, while retaining when each statement was believed and why. Avoid both stale answers and rewriting history.
status: LongMemEval includes knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning challenges. A robust memory model must distinguish correction, change, contradiction, and uncertainty.
why: Supports dependable long-term assistance and auditability.
key_works: Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory*, arXiv:2410.10813.

title: Lifetime memory under bounded operating cost
open: Maintain useful memory across years of interaction with bounded per-query cost and controlled degradation. Include changes in models, schemas, storage backends, and user identity relationships.
status: Long-conversation benchmarks and memory-managed agents provide shorter-horizon building blocks. Multi-year operational continuity is a larger systems target.
why: Enables assistants whose usefulness accumulates rather than resets.
key_works: Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753; Packer et al., 2023, *MemGPT*, arXiv:2310.08560.

title: Precise memory deletion without collateral forgetting
open: Remove a specified fact or experience from retrievable and parametric memory while preserving unrelated knowledge. Verify deletion against paraphrases, inference, and later updates.
status: ROME and MEMIT demonstrate targeted editing; TOFU benchmarks unlearning. Editing an answer and eliminating recoverable information are not equivalent.
why: Supports user corrections, privacy requests, and removal of poisoned memories.
key_works: Meng et al., 2022, *Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT*, arXiv:2202.05262; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

title: Memory access control with inference-aware boundaries
open: Enforce who may use each memory across users, agents, organizations, and delegated tasks. Prevent unauthorized disclosure through summaries or inferences, not only direct record access.
status: Agent memory and tool-security research provide separate components. Their composition requires policies that survive retrieval, summarization, and delegation.
why: Makes persistent assistants usable in shared and regulated environments.
key_works: Packer et al., 2023, *MemGPT*, arXiv:2310.08560; Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813.

title: Realistic longitudinal memory evaluation
open: Build consented, longitudinal evaluations containing forgotten details, changed preferences, contradictory reports, multiple people, and meaningful consequences for errors. Prevent answers from being recoverable through superficial lexical cues.
status: LoCoMo and LongMemEval are concrete 2024 baselines. Longer, more representative and privacy-preserving evaluations remain an expansion target.
why: Separates genuine long-term assistance from benchmark-specific retrieval tricks.
key_works: Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753; Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813.

title: Semantic rather than token-level calibration
open: Assign calibrated confidence to propositions and decisions despite multiple equivalent phrasings. Confidence should not change arbitrarily because one answer requires more tokens.
status: Semantic uncertainty methods were introduced in 2023. Robust calibration across domains, generation styles, and correlated claims remains broader.
why: Makes confidence useful to people and downstream systems.
key_works: Kuhn, Gal, and Farquhar, 2023, *Semantic Uncertainty*, arXiv:2302.09664; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

title: Separating missing knowledge from irreducible ambiguity
open: Distinguish uncertainty caused by insufficient model knowledge from uncertainty inherent in the question, evidence, or world. Use that distinction to choose retrieval, clarification, experimentation, or abstention.
status: Semantic uncertainty captures variation in meaning, but variation alone does not identify its causal source.
why: Selects the right remedy instead of merely reporting low confidence.
key_works: Kuhn et al., 2023, *Semantic Uncertainty*, arXiv:2302.09664; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

title: Propagating uncertainty through dependent reasoning steps
open: Estimate end-to-end uncertainty when intermediate claims, retrieved evidence, and tools have correlated errors. Avoid multiplying unjustified independent confidence estimates.
status: Existing confidence and multi-hop retrieval methods address components. Reliable uncertainty composition across adaptive reasoning remains a distinct challenge.
why: Prevents long reasoning chains from presenting false precision.
key_works: Kuhn et al., 2023, *Semantic Uncertainty*, arXiv:2302.09664; Trivedi et al., 2022/2023, *Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2212.10509.

title: Conformal guarantees under adaptive interaction
open: Extend useful prediction-set or abstention guarantees to conversations where queries, retrieved data, and model updates depend on earlier outputs. State the dependence assumptions explicitly.
status: Conformal language modeling provides finite-sample guarantees under specified sampling conditions. Adaptive deployment can violate the assumptions supporting ordinary coverage.
why: Makes statistical guarantees relevant to actual interactive assistants.
key_works: Quach et al., 2023/2024, *Conformal Language Modeling*, arXiv:2306.10193.

title: Out-of-distribution abstention with useful coverage
open: Detect unfamiliar situations and abstain at a controlled error rate without refusing most useful work. Evaluate shifts not represented in the abstention system’s development data.
status: Open-set recognition and LLM confidence estimation supply partial methods. Useful coverage under genuinely novel shifts is stronger than thresholding a familiar benchmark.
why: Enables graceful failure when a model encounters conditions outside its competence.
key_works: Bendale and Boult, 2015/2016, *Towards Open Set Deep Networks*, arXiv:1511.06233; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

title: Hallucination–abstention–retrieval lower bounds
open: Derive sharp achievable frontiers among factual error, abstention, retrieval cost, and coverage under explicit information assumptions. Do not treat a bound for arbitrary unobserved facts as a universal impossibility of truthful assistance.
status: Kalai and Vempala established a calibrated-model hallucination result in 2023–2024. Systems with retrieval, restricted claims, and abstention require a richer characterization.
why: Identifies which reliability promises are feasible.
key_works: Kalai and Vempala, 2023/2024, *Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate*, arXiv:2311.14648; Lewis et al., 2020, *Retrieval-Augmented Generation*, arXiv:2005.11401.

title: Ambiguity-aware confidence and clarification
open: Recognize when several interpretations of a user request are plausible and identify the smallest clarification that changes the decision. Avoid confidently answering one interpretation without disclosure.
status: Semantic uncertainty supplies relevant measurements, but ambiguity over user intent is not identical to uncertainty over factual answers.
why: Prevents confidently executing the wrong task.
key_works: Kuhn et al., 2023, *Semantic Uncertainty*, arXiv:2302.09664; Liang et al., 2022, *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models*, arXiv:2211.09110.

title: Calibration preservation after deployment modifications
open: Maintain or cheaply restore calibrated confidence after quantization, distillation, routing, retrieval changes, and fine-tuning. Detect changes that leave average accuracy intact but damage uncertainty estimates.
status: Compression methods demonstrate strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs; confidence estimation is usually a separate measurement problem.
why: Keeps downstream risk controls valid after routine optimization.
key_works: Lin et al., 2023, *AWQ*, arXiv:2306.00978; Frantar et al., 2022, *GPTQ*, arXiv:2210.17323; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

title: Contamination-resistant evaluation over repeated model generations
open: Maintain evaluations that remain informative after repeated public releases and model-training cycles. Separate genuine improvement from adaptation to the benchmark’s generation process.
status: LiveBench introduced regularly refreshed, contamination-limited evaluation in 2024. Refreshing examples alone does not guarantee independence from recurring templates.
why: Preserves the meaning of progress measurements.
key_works: White et al., 2024, *LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Limited LLM Benchmark*, arXiv:2406.19314.

title: Predicting real deployment outcomes from benchmarks
open: Determine which benchmark measurements predict error rates, productivity, user benefit, and harm in actual deployments. Validate the mapping prospectively across organizations and model updates.
status: HELM broadens evaluation dimensions, while realistic agent benchmarks move closer to workflows. External validity still requires field validation rather than assumed transfer.
why: Stops organizations from optimizing scores that do not predict useful outcomes.
key_works: Liang et al., 2022, *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models*, arXiv:2211.09110; Yao et al., 2024, *τ-bench*, arXiv:2406.12045.

title: Unbiased and auditable model judges
open: Evaluate generated work without systematically favoring verbosity, familiar model styles, answer position, or the judge’s own family. Detect judge manipulation and quantify disagreement with expert adjudication.
status: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena work documented strengths and limitations of LLM judges in 2023. Better agreement on some tasks does not eliminate structural bias.
why: Makes scalable evaluation less vulnerable to self-reinforcing scoring artifacts.
key_works: Zheng et al., 2023, *Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena*, arXiv:2306.05685.

title: Metamorphic tests for semantic invariance
open: Generate transformations that should preserve an answer or change it in a precisely known way, then detect violations. Cover paraphrase, units, entity renaming, document order, and irrelevant context.
status: Compositional and long-context benchmarks expose selected invariance failures. A systematic transformation library with validated semantic preservation remains a useful missing infrastructure.
why: Finds brittle behavior without requiring a new gold answer for every example.
key_works: Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610; Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle*, arXiv:2307.03172.

title: Full-lifecycle cost accounting for AI capability
open: Compare systems using training, tuning, failed attempts, inference, retrieval, human review, and maintenance costs. Prevent hidden teacher or search costs from disappearing behind a favorable final-run number.
status: Inference-aware scaling and deployment-energy measurement address important components. A consistently adopted lifecycle comparison protocol remains a separate target.
why: Makes economic and efficiency claims comparable.
key_works: Bian et al., 2025, *Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models*, arXiv:2501.18107; Luccioni, Jernite, and Strubell, 2023/2024, *Power Hungry Processing*, arXiv:2311.16863.

title: Repeatability rather than best-of-run success
open: Measure the probability of reliable success across repeated executions, environments, seeds, and minor perturbations. Report failure distributions instead of highlighting a single successful trajectory.
status: τ-bench emphasizes repeated reliability; ReliabilityBench added production-like stress evaluation in 2026. Broader standardized repeatability testing remains valuable.
why: Distinguishes impressive demonstrations from dependable services.
key_works: Yao et al., 2024, *τ-bench*, arXiv:2406.12045; Gupta, 2026, *ReliabilityBench*, arXiv:2601.06112.

title: Measuring cumulative failure in long deployments
open: Estimate how small per-action errors accumulate over weeks of operation, including correlated failures, recovery, and delayed discovery. Build evaluations that reveal unrecoverable damage, not just task completion.
status: Long-horizon agent and stress benchmarks provide shorter controlled tests. Long-duration cumulative-risk measurement remains a distinct experimental program.
why: Helps set realistic autonomy limits and supervision requirements.
key_works: Gupta, 2026, *ReliabilityBench*, arXiv:2601.06112; Cemri et al., 2025, *Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?*, arXiv:2503.13657.

title: Measuring general skill-acquisition efficiency
open: Evaluate how efficiently a system acquires unfamiliar skills from limited experience, controlling prior exposure and task-specific engineering. Include interactive exploration rather than only static puzzle answers.
status: Chollet formalized the distinction between skill and skill-acquisition efficiency in 2019. ARC Prize 2026 includes static and interactive tracks, providing concrete but not exhaustive tests.
why: Makes “general intelligence” claims more operational and less dependent on memorized skill coverage.
key_works: Chollet, 2019, *On the Measure of Intelligence*, arXiv:1911.01547; ARC Prize Foundation, 2026, *ARC Prize 2026*.
prize: Related competition: **$2 million across three ARC Prize 2026 tracks**, not a bounty for resolving this entire research problem.

title: Recovering a sufficiently complete feature basis
open: Recover the features needed to explain a model’s behavior, including rare, distributed, nonlinear, and context-dependent features. Quantify what explanatory content remains missing.
status: Sparse autoencoders and superposition models provide major 2022–2024 foundations. Interpretable recovered features do not establish completeness.
why: Prevents interpretability conclusions from depending only on the features easiest to detect.
key_works: Elhage et al., 2022, *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652; Cunningham et al., 2023, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models*, arXiv:2309.08600.

title: Identifiability of learned interpretability features
open: Determine when different feature decompositions represent the same underlying computation and when they imply incompatible explanations. Supply uncertainty or equivalence classes rather than treating one dictionary as canonical.
status: Sparse-autoencoder research establishes useful decompositions and scaling methods. Nonuniqueness and dependence on training choices remain important residual questions.
why: Makes feature-level scientific claims reproducible.
key_works: Cunningham et al., 2023, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features*, arXiv:2309.08600; Gao et al., 2024, *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders*, arXiv:2406.04093.

title: Universality of circuits across models
open: Identify which computational mechanisms recur across seeds, scales, architectures, and languages. Distinguish true shared algorithms from superficially similar activation patterns.
status: Feature extraction and circuit tracing permit concrete comparisons. A general account of which mechanisms are universal versus contingent remains open.
why: Allows interpretability findings to transfer beyond one checkpoint.
key_works: Gao et al., 2024, *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders*, arXiv:2406.04093; Ameisen et al., 2025, *Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models*.

title: Causally faithful circuit extraction
open: Extract circuits that predict the effects of interventions on the original model, not merely an interpretable approximation. Include attention routing, nonlinear interactions, and mechanisms suppressed by a chosen prompt.
status: The 2025 circuit-tracing method uses replacement models and validates interventions while explicitly discussing missing attention mechanisms and reconstruction limitations.
why: Turns explanatory diagrams into testable causal models.
key_works: Ameisen et al., 2025, *Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models*, Transformer Circuits.

title: Whole-model explanation at practical cost
open: Explain a substantial fraction of a deployed model’s important behaviors with bounded analysis cost, including rare failures. Provide coverage metrics rather than a collection of selected case studies.
status: Sparse-autoencoder scaling reached millions of latents, and circuit tracing supports detailed examples. Comprehensive coverage is a different scale and evaluation problem.
why: Could make interpretability a routine assurance tool rather than bespoke research.
key_works: Gao et al., 2024, *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders*, arXiv:2406.04093; Ameisen et al., 2025, *Circuit Tracing*.

title: Detecting covert computation in reasoning channels
open: Detect when internal or external reasoning representations carry task-relevant information that is not captured by their apparent natural-language meaning. Evaluate latent and textual channels without assuming all hidden computation is malicious.
status: Faithfulness studies establish that visible reasoning can omit causal influences; latent-reasoning systems make the representational issue explicit.
why: Clarifies what reasoning logs can and cannot reveal.
key_works: Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702; Hao et al., 2024, *Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space*, arXiv:2412.06769.

title: Faithful natural-language explanations
open: Generate explanations whose stated reasons correspond to factors that actually caused the answer. Distinguish retrospective rationalization from a faithful account using interventions.
status: 2023 studies demonstrated unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations and proposed tests. Fluent reasoning remains insufficient evidence of faithfulness.
why: Makes explanations useful for debugging and justified trust.
key_works: Turpin et al., 2023, *Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think*, arXiv:2305.04388; Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702.

title: Behavior steering with bounded collateral effects
open: Modify a target behavior through internal interventions while bounding effects on unrelated capabilities and contexts. Detect when the intervention’s meaning changes under distribution shift.
status: Feature-based interventions and circuit tracing provide mechanisms for steering. Broad preservation guarantees and reliable out-of-distribution semantics remain open.
why: Could make targeted model correction safer than broad retraining.
key_works: Cunningham et al., 2023, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features*, arXiv:2309.08600; Ameisen et al., 2025, *Circuit Tracing*.

title: Weak-to-strong supervision without inherited blind spots
open: Use weaker evaluators to train stronger systems while reducing, rather than reproducing, the evaluator’s systematic errors. Demonstrate transfer to tasks where the supervisor cannot directly verify the answer.
status: Weak-to-strong generalization experiments were introduced in 2023. They establish a research direction, not a general solution to supervising more capable systems.
why: Addresses supervision when direct human evaluation becomes inadequate.
key_works: Burns et al., 2023, *Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision*, arXiv:2312.09390.

title: Debate with bounded and manipulable judges
open: Determine when adversarial debate helps a limited judge reach the truth, including strategic omission, persuasion, unequal debater capabilities, and unverifiable claims.
status: AI safety via debate was proposed in 2018. Idealized arguments do not settle effectiveness with real human or model judges.
why: Tests a proposed route to scalable oversight.
key_works: Irving, Christiano, and Amodei, 2018, *AI safety via debate*, arXiv:1805.00899.

title: Oversight decomposition without losing global errors
open: Break complex work into reviewable pieces while preserving detection of errors that arise only through interactions among pieces. Specify when local approval implies acceptable global behavior.
status: Debate and weak-to-strong supervision motivate decomposition. Neither automatically supplies compositional guarantees for open-ended work.
why: Makes scalable review possible without hiding failures between task boundaries.
key_works: Irving et al., 2018, *AI safety via debate*, arXiv:1805.00899; Burns et al., 2023, *Weak-to-Strong Generalization*, arXiv:2312.09390.

title: Detecting learned objectives distinct from training objectives
open: Identify when a trained system implements a persistent optimization process whose effective objective differs from the intended objective. Separate robust evidence from anthropomorphic interpretation of outputs.
status: The mesa-optimization framing dates to 2019. Operationally diagnosing such objectives in realistic systems remains difficult.
why: Supports earlier detection of behavior that generalizes undesirably.
key_works: Hubinger et al., 2019, *Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems*, arXiv:1906.01820.

title: Reliable detection of strategic deception
open: Detect strategically misleading behavior under a specified threat model without relying on the model’s self-report. Distinguish deliberate concealment from error, role-play, or ambiguous instructions.
status: Sleeper Agents demonstrated persistence of deliberately constructed deceptive behaviors through some safety training in 2024. That does not imply every deployed model is deceptive.
why: Makes evaluations more robust to systems that behave differently under scrutiny.
key_works: Hubinger et al., 2024, *Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training*, arXiv:2401.05566.

title: Corrigibility under learning and delegation
open: Maintain willingness to accept correction, shutdown, and goal revision as systems learn, plan, and delegate. Define guarantees that do not depend on simplistic assumptions about perfect human rationality.
status: The Off-Switch Game provides a formal 2016–2017 treatment of a restricted setting. Persistent, learning, multi-agent systems require broader analysis.
why: Preserves meaningful human control as autonomy increases.
key_works: Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016/2017, *The Off-Switch Game*, arXiv:1611.08219; Hubinger et al., 2019, *Risks from Learned Optimization*, arXiv:1906.01820.

title: Preventing long-horizon specification gaming
open: Detect and prevent plans that satisfy a local metric while undermining the larger objective through delayed side effects, manipulation of measurement, or shifting costs elsewhere.
status: Reward overoptimization and learned-optimization research identify core mechanisms. Long-horizon tool environments add opportunities not captured by short response evaluations.
why: Protects real objectives when agents can alter the environment.
key_works: Gao et al., 2022, *Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization*, arXiv:2210.10760; Hubinger et al., 2019, *Risks from Learned Optimization*, arXiv:1906.01820.

title: Legitimate pluralistic alignment mechanisms
open: Design governance and training procedures that represent affected communities, preserve principled disagreement, and make trade-offs contestable. Evaluate legitimacy and outcomes rather than treating preference averaging as sufficient.
status: A 2024 roadmap explicitly frames pluralistic alignment as a multi-part agenda. Scalable institutional mechanisms remain unresolved.
why: Avoids embedding one provider’s preferences as an unchallengeable universal standard.
key_works: Sorensen et al., 2024, *A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment*, arXiv:2402.05070.

title: Indirect prompt-injection resistance with preserved utility
open: Prevent untrusted documents, webpages, messages, and tool outputs from changing an agent’s authorized goals or permissions. Demonstrate resistance under adaptive attacks while retaining useful document processing.
status: Indirect injection was documented in 2023; AgentDojo and CaMeL provide evaluation and architectural defenses. Utility-preserving coverage across heterogeneous applications remains broader.
why: Protects agents that must read adversarially supplied information.
key_works: Greshake et al., 2023, *Not what you’ve signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173; Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813.

title: Multimodal instruction-authority separation
open: Preserve the distinction between instructions and data across images, audio, video, OCR text, and embedded metadata. Prevent authority from being laundered through modality conversion.
status: Text-based injection research establishes the trust-boundary problem; multimodal systems expand the input surface. A unified cross-modal authority model is the target.
why: Prevents a screenshot, recording, or document from acquiring unintended control privileges.
key_works: Greshake et al., 2023, *Not what you’ve signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173; Debenedetti et al., 2024, *AgentDojo*, arXiv:2406.13352.

title: Persistent-memory poisoning detection
open: Detect and quarantine malicious or erroneous information before it becomes trusted long-term memory, including gradual poisoning spread across many interactions.
status: Memory systems and prompt-injection benchmarks provide separate foundations. Persistence changes the threat from one bad answer to future behavioral contamination.
why: Protects agents whose future decisions depend on accumulated experience.
key_works: Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813; Debenedetti et al., 2024, *AgentDojo*, arXiv:2406.13352.

title: Confused-deputy prevention across agent delegation
open: Ensure delegated agents and tools cannot exercise privileges beyond the originating user’s authorized intent. Preserve scope, purpose, and revocation through nested delegation.
status: Capability-aware defenses such as CaMeL address important information-flow boundaries. Multi-agent delegation adds cross-process and cross-principal composition requirements.
why: Prevents apparently legitimate tool calls from becoming unauthorized actions.
key_works: Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813; Wu et al., 2023, *AutoGen*, arXiv:2308.08155.

title: Exfiltration control for useful tool-using agents
open: Prevent sensitive information from leaving through unauthorized destinations, including indirect encoding and derived summaries, while allowing legitimate communication and analysis.
status: Information-flow-oriented agent defenses supply a concrete direction. General semantic leakage control is harder than blocking a small set of literal secrets.
why: Makes agents safe to connect to private organizational data.
key_works: Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813; Greshake et al., 2023, *Not what you’ve signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173.

title: Detecting poisoning across the model supply chain
open: Detect harmful modifications introduced through datasets, checkpoints, adapters, retrieval indexes, or tools, including changes that activate only under rare conditions.
status: Sleeper-agent experiments show persistence of constructed conditional behaviors; provenance audits expose difficulties in tracing training inputs. End-to-end supply-chain assurance combines both concerns.
why: Supports safe reuse of external model and data components.
key_works: Hubinger et al., 2024, *Sleeper Agents*, arXiv:2401.05566; Longpre et al., 2023, *The Data Provenance Initiative*, arXiv:2310.16787.

title: Robustness bounds against adaptive jailbreaks
open: Establish meaningful robustness guarantees against explicitly bounded adaptive attackers while retaining useful responses. Characterize impossibility frontiers when attacker access or utility requirements make a guarantee unattainable.
status: Transferable adversarial attacks were demonstrated in 2023. Empirical resistance to a fixed attack set is not a guarantee against adaptive search.
why: Replaces unqualified “jailbreak-proof” claims with defensible threat models.
key_works: Zou et al., 2023, *Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models*, arXiv:2307.15043; Debenedetti et al., 2024, *AgentDojo*, arXiv:2406.13352.

title: Containment that survives useful autonomy
open: Keep an agent within authorized resources and effects while permitting realistic coding, browsing, communication, and tool installation. Evaluate escape prevention, credential handling, and operational usability together.
status: Agent operating systems and tool-security architectures provide components. A sandbox boundary alone does not define permissible external effects.
why: Allows useful autonomy without treating all generated actions as trustworthy.
key_works: Mei et al., 2024, *AIOS: LLM Agent Operating System*, arXiv:2403.16971; Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813.

title: Valid membership-inference audits
open: Measure whether a model reveals training membership while controlling for distribution mismatch, duplicates, and public availability. Report false-positive rates suitable for consequential claims.
status: Membership inference has a foundational 2016–2017 literature; LLM data extraction provides a related but different privacy signal.
why: Prevents both overlooked privacy leakage and unsupported accusations of training use.
key_works: Shokri et al., 2016/2017, *Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1610.05820; Carlini et al., 2020/2021, *Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models*, arXiv:2012.07805.

title: Bounding extraction risk beyond observed attacks
open: Estimate or bound the probability that sensitive training content can be extracted by adaptive users, including rare memorized sequences. Distinguish failure to find an attack from evidence of safety.
status: Training-data extraction was demonstrated in 2020–2021. Finite attack suites do not exhaust the space of possible queries.
why: Supports defensible privacy decisions before model release.
key_works: Carlini et al., 2020/2021, *Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models*, arXiv:2012.07805; Abadi et al., 2016, *Deep Learning with Differential Privacy*, arXiv:1607.00133.

title: Differential privacy with broad language-model utility
open: Improve the privacy–utility–compute frontier for language-model training, including rare facts and minority-language performance. Specify the protected unit and account for all training stages.
status: Differentially private deep learning has established methods since 2016. Strong guarantees with competitive broad utility remain a demanding scaling target.
why: Makes useful learning from sensitive data more feasible.
key_works: Abadi et al., 2016, *Deep Learning with Differential Privacy*, arXiv:1607.00133.

title: Federated language learning under real heterogeneity
open: Train or adapt language models across nonidentically distributed clients with intermittent availability, privacy constraints, and adversarial contributions. Avoid improvements for dominant clients masking regressions for others.
status: Federated averaging established an influential baseline in 2016–2017. Large-language-model workloads add substantial communication, personalization, and privacy complications.
why: Enables collaboration without centralizing all raw data.
key_works: McMahan et al., 2016/2017, *Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data*, arXiv:1602.05629; Abadi et al., 2016, *Deep Learning with Differential Privacy*, arXiv:1607.00133.

title: Certified unlearning for practically trained LLMs
open: Remove specified training contributions with a certificate meaningfully related to retraining without those contributions. Preserve utility and avoid requiring full retraining for every request.
status: Certified removal exists for restricted model classes; TOFU supplies an LLM unlearning benchmark. Behavioral suppression alone is not a certified removal result.
why: Makes deletion requests technically meaningful.
key_works: Guo et al., 2019/2020, *Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1911.03030; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

title: Unlearning that survives later training
open: Ensure removed information does not reappear after unrelated fine-tuning, model merging, memory retrieval, or exposure to correlated examples. Define when relearning from genuinely new authorized data is permissible.
status: Unlearning benchmarks and large-scale editing methods address immediate behavior. Durability across a model’s subsequent lifecycle is an additional requirement.
why: Prevents deletion from being a temporary surface effect.
key_works: Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121; Meng et al., 2022/2023, *Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer*, arXiv:2210.07229.

title: Privacy-preserving retrieval and generation
open: Answer over private corpora without unnecessarily revealing queries, retrieved records, access patterns, or derived sensitive facts to infrastructure operators and other tenants.
status: Secure multiparty computation and RAG provide separate foundations. Combining them with realistic latency, dynamic indexes, and authorization is the target.
why: Enables confidential assistants without assuming every service operator is trusted.
key_works: Knott et al., 2021, *CrypTen: Secure Multi-Party Computation Meets Machine Learning*, arXiv:2109.00984; Lewis et al., 2020, *Retrieval-Augmented Generation*, arXiv:2005.11401.

title: Low-overhead confidential model inference
open: Execute useful large-model inference with cryptographic or hardware-backed confidentiality while accounting for metadata leakage, malicious participants, and side channels. Reduce overhead enough for interactive workloads.
status: CrypTen demonstrates accessible secure multiparty neural computation. Full-scale interactive language inference imposes substantially larger state and communication demands.
why: Could make confidential AI a default deployment option.
key_works: Knott et al., 2021, *CrypTen: Secure Multi-Party Computation Meets Machine Learning*, arXiv:2109.00984.

title: Low-resource language capability parity
open: Close capability gaps on reasoning, instruction following, factuality, and tool use—not merely translation—without requiring web-scale corpora in every language.
status: NLLB demonstrated broad translation coverage in 2022; linguistic-inclusion research documents uneven resource availability. General assistant parity is a wider target.
why: Makes advanced AI useful beyond high-resource language communities.
key_works: NLLB Team, 2022, *No Language Left Behind*, arXiv:2207.04672; Joshi et al., 2020, *The State and Fate of Linguistic Diversity and Inclusion in the NLP World*, arXiv:2004.09095.

title: Equalizing tokenization-induced cost and context limits
open: Reduce systematic differences in cost, latency, and effective context capacity caused by how languages are tokenized. Evaluate both technical efficiency and semantic performance.
status: Tokenizer-induced language disparities were quantified in 2023. Byte-level adaptive modeling provides an alternative but does not automatically establish parity.
why: Prevents infrastructure pricing and limits from penalizing language choice.
key_works: Petrov et al., 2023, *Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages*, arXiv:2305.15425; Pagnoni et al., 2024, *Byte Latent Transformer*, arXiv:2412.09871.

title: Eliminating consequential dialect discrimination
open: Prevent dialect features from causing unjustified differences in judgments about competence, character, employability, or risk. Test realistic downstream decisions rather than only explicit stereotype prompts.
status: Hofmann et al. documented consequential dialect prejudice in 2024. Removing overtly prejudiced language is not equivalent to removing decision-level discrimination.
why: Protects users whose language varieties differ from dominant training norms.
