key_works: Joshi et al., 2020, *The State and Fate of Linguistic Diversity and Inclusion in the NLP World*, arXiv:2004.09095; Longpre et al., 2024, *Bridging the Data Provenance Gap*, arXiv:2412.17847.

title: Funding longitudinal evaluation as a public good
open: Support multi-year, independent evaluations of AI’s effects on work, learning, relationships, and safety, including model-version tracking and access to deployment data.
status: Existing human-outcome studies demonstrate feasible short-term designs. Longitudinal evaluation requires funding and access arrangements that outlast individual product cycles.
why: Reveals delayed effects that short benchmarks and launch studies cannot detect.
key_works: Fang et al., 2025, *How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use*, arXiv:2503.17473; Bastani et al., 2024/2025, *Generative AI Without Guardrails Can Harm Learning*, SSRN:4895486.

title: A privacy-preserving incident-data commons
open: Create mechanisms for sharing failures, near misses, and remediation outcomes across organizations without exposing victims, confidential data, or exploitable details.
status: The AI Incident Database shows the value of shared case collection. Confidential reporting, standardized severity, and validated remediation require further infrastructure.
why: Allows organizations to learn from one another’s failures instead of repeating them.
key_works: McGregor, 2020/2021, *Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents*, arXiv:2011.08512; Brundage et al., 2020, *Toward Trustworthy AI Development*, arXiv:2004.07213.

title: Evidence-based open-weight release decisions
open: Evaluate the benefits and risks of releasing model weights under explicit scenarios, including independent research, concentration, downstream modification, and misuse. Develop criteria that can be updated with evidence.
status: Foundation-model risk and transparency frameworks identify relevant dimensions. No single openness label resolves the trade-offs for all models and deployment contexts.
why: Replaces categorical release debates with testable, context-sensitive decisions.
key_works: Bommasani et al., 2021, *On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models*, arXiv:2108.07258; Bommasani et al., 2023, *The Foundation Model Transparency Index*, arXiv:2310.12941.

title: Credible compensation and attribution for training contributions
open: Design compensation or attribution mechanisms that remain meaningful when data is duplicated, transformed, complementary, or only indirectly influential. Resist strategic duplication and unverifiable ownership claims.
status: Data-provenance audits and influence estimation provide partial technical foundations. Fair and manipulation-resistant allocation remains an economic and institutional problem.
why: Supports sustainable data supply and more legitimate model development.
key_works: Longpre et al., 2023, *The Data Provenance Initiative*, arXiv:2310.16787; Koh and Liang, 2017, *Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions*, arXiv:1703.04730.

title: Independently auditable AI footprint standards
open: Establish interoperable reporting and audit methods for energy, water, emissions, hardware lifecycle, and workload allocation. Make uncertainty and omitted components visible.
status: Research methods exist for deployment energy, water estimates, and embodied carbon. Comparable mandatory or voluntary reporting needs institutional coordination and verification.
why: Makes environmental claims accountable and comparable across providers.
key_works: Luccioni et al., 2023/2024, *Power Hungry Processing*, arXiv:2311.16863; Li et al., 2023, *Making AI Less “Thirsty”*, arXiv:2304.03271; Gupta et al., 2020/2021, *Chasing Carbon*, arXiv:2011.02839.

title: International verification of consequential AI commitments
open: Design technically and politically workable ways to verify agreed claims about model development, evaluation, access controls, or deployment without requiring unrestricted disclosure of sensitive information.
status: Verifiable-claim mechanisms and transparency indexes provide building blocks. Cross-border verification, incentives, and enforceability remain broader institutional problems.
why: Makes cooperation depend less on unverifiable assurances.
key_works: Brundage et al., 2020, *Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims*, arXiv:2004.07213; Bommasani et al., 2023, *The Foundation Model Transparency Index*, arXiv:2310.12941.
